## The assignment

In class we built a house price model for Philadelphia. Now your team does it for a city you haven't modeled: **Chicago**.

The Cook County Assessor's Office has to value every home in the county, including the vast majority that didn't sell this year. Assessments drive property tax bills. When they're wrong in a systematic way, some households pay more than their share. A 2017 *Chicago Tribune* investigation, "The Tax Divide," found exactly that in Cook County: lower-value homes were assessed at higher shares of their worth than expensive ones.

Build a model that predicts **single-family sale prices in Chicago, 2023–2025**, using only the tools from this course. The file contains **only features of the house itself**. Everything about location is yours to build.

### A real test

| File | What's in it |
|---|---|
| `chicago_train.csv` | About 80% of the houses, **with** sale prices |
| `chicago_test.csv` | The other 20%, **without** sale prices. You predict them; we score you. |

The test houses were held out by house, not by sale, so a house that sold twice is entirely on one side. Your CV RMSE is your estimate. Your test RMSE is the truth. **If they're far apart, something leaked.** 

**Due:** Friday, October 30. All teammates renders the file on their portfolio and every member submits that link on Canvas. One teammate uploads `team_YNN_predictions.csv`.

**Individual accountability:** Q7 on October 30 asks each of you about *this* model: which features you used and why, your CV and test RMSE, and where the model fails worst. Make sure everyone can explain all of it.

These helpers are to help you get off the ground.

```{.r .cell-code}
check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")
  }
}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)
  st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
}
```

## Part 1: Clean and explore

Decide which training sales are market sales. Record each rule, why, and how many it removed. Then explore: at least four plots, including a map of price.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
train_raw <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "train")
n0 <- nrow(train_raw)

# Rule 1: sales of $1 or less are transfers, not market sales
step1 <- train_raw %>% filter(sale_price > 1)

# Rule 2: sales of $5 million or more (the top 0.1%)
step2 <- step1 %>% filter(sale_price < 5000000)

# Rule 3: more than 4 fireplaces (NAs kept, they are filled with 0 in Part 2)
step3 <- step2 %>% filter(is.na(num_fireplaces) | num_fireplaces <= 4)

# Rule 4: lots larger than 3 acres
step4 <- step3 %>% filter(is.na(lotsize_acre) | lotsize_acre <= 3)

# Rule 5: negative building age is a data error (age 0 = new construction, kept)
step5 <- step4 %>% filter(is.na(building_age) | building_age >= 0)

cleaning_log <- tibble(
  rule    = c("Sale price <= $1",
              "Sale price >= $5,000,000",
              "More than 4 fireplaces",
              "Lot larger than 3 acres",
              "Negative building age"),
  why     = c("Transfers between family members or entities, not market sales",
              "Top 0.1% of sales; a few mansions would pull the whole model",
              "Estate-type homes; too few to learn from",
              "Not a typical city lot; likely mis-coded or not a single-family sale",
              "Impossible value, data entry error"),
  removed = c(n0 - nrow(step1),
              nrow(step1) - nrow(step2),
              nrow(step2) - nrow(step3),
              nrow(step3) - nrow(step4),
              nrow(step4) - nrow(step5))
)
print(cleaning_log)
```

**Answer:** What in your exploration shaped your modeling choices?

*Your answer:*

Our five cleaning rules removed 39 of 23,200 training sales (see the table above): 30 sales of $5 million or more, 8 homes with more than 4 fireplaces and 1 lot over 3 acres. We checked for $1 transfers and negative ages and found none (the cheapest sale is about $10,000). We kept rows with missing values and filled them instead, and we kept new construction (age 0).

Our first draft also dropped every sale over $1 million. The histogram changed our minds: those 1,892 sales are 8.2% of the training data, not a few outliers, and the test houses are not cleaned, so the model has to price them. Dropping them made CV RMSE look good only because the hardest homes were gone. We now drop only the top 0.1% (over $5 million).

Two other things from the plots shaped the model. The price map shows a clear north/south split, with higher prices on the North Side and near the lake. A model built only on house features cannot see that, so we knew we would need location features. And the age plot is U-shaped: new homes sell highest, prices bottom out for homes 50–100 years old, and rise again for the oldest (historic) homes. So we added age squared.

---

## Part 2: Build the model

Start with a structure-only baseline. Then add features in steps you can learn from, logging each one. Keep the log in a tibble with columns `model`, `added`, `cv_rmse`, `moran_i`, `notes`.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Fill NAs in house features on all_sales (Rule 1: fill, never drop test rows)
all_sales <- all_sales %>%
  mutate(num_fireplaces = replace_na(num_fireplaces, 0),
         building_000sf = replace_na(building_000sf, median(building_000sf, na.rm = TRUE)),
         building_age   = replace_na(building_age,   median(building_age,   na.rm = TRUE)),
         lotsize_acre   = replace_na(lotsize_acre,   median(lotsize_acre,   na.rm = TRUE)),
         num_bedrooms   = replace_na(num_bedrooms,   median(num_bedrooms,   na.rm = TRUE)))

# Feature 1: distance to the Loop (State & Madison), in miles
loop <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-87.6278, 41.8820)), crs = 4326) %>% st_transform(3435)
all_sales <- all_sales %>%
  mutate(dist_loop_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(geometry, loop)) / 5280)

# Feature 2: census tract income and poverty (ACS 2023 5-year)
acs <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract", state = "IL", county = "Cook", year = 2023,
  variables = c(med_inc = "B19013_001",
                pov     = "B17001_002",
                pov_den = "B17001_001"),     # population for whom poverty is determined
  geometry = TRUE, output = "wide") %>%
  mutate(med_inc = med_incE,
         pct_pov = 100 * povE / pov_denE) %>%
  select(GEOID, med_inc, pct_pov) %>%
  st_transform(3435)

all_sales <- all_sales %>%
  st_join(acs, join = st_nearest_feature) %>%
  mutate(med_inc = replace_na(med_inc, median(med_inc, na.rm = TRUE)),
         pct_pov = replace_na(pct_pov, median(pct_pov, na.rm = TRUE)))

# Feature 3: community area (fixed effect). Dataset igwz-8jzy on the Data Portal.
# If the join below errors, run names(ca) to check the name column.
ca <- st_read("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/igwz-8jzy.geojson", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  select(community) %>%
  st_transform(3435)

all_sales <- all_sales %>%
  st_join(ca, join = st_nearest_feature)

# Split training sales off again, with the Part 1 cleaning applied
train <- all_sales %>% filter(row_id %in% keep_ids)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
f1 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + lotsize_acre
f2 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + lotsize_acre + num_bedrooms + num_fireplaces
f3 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + lotsize_acre + log1p(num_bedrooms) + num_fireplaces
f4 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + I(building_age^2) + lotsize_acre +
  log1p(num_bedrooms) + num_fireplaces
f5 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + I(building_age^2) + lotsize_acre +
  log1p(num_bedrooms) + num_fireplaces + dist_loop_mi
f6 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + I(building_age^2) + lotsize_acre +
  log1p(num_bedrooms) + num_fireplaces + dist_loop_mi + log(med_inc) + pct_pov
f7 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + I(building_age^2) + lotsize_acre +
  log1p(num_bedrooms) + num_fireplaces + dist_loop_mi + log(med_inc) + pct_pov + community

# CV RMSE
rmse1 <- cv_rmse(f1, train)
rmse2 <- cv_rmse(f2, train)
rmse3 <- cv_rmse(f3, train)
rmse4 <- cv_rmse(f4, train)
rmse5 <- cv_rmse(f5, train)
rmse6 <- cv_rmse(f6, train)
rmse7 <- cv_rmse(f7, train)

# Spatial weights: 5 nearest neighbors, projected coordinates (feet)
coords <- st_coordinates(train)
nb <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 5))
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W")

# Moran's I on out-of-fold residuals (same predictions the CV RMSE is based on)
r1 <- train$sale_price - cv_pred(f1, train)
r2 <- train$sale_price - cv_pred(f2, train)
r3 <- train$sale_price - cv_pred(f3, train)
r4 <- train$sale_price - cv_pred(f4, train)
r5 <- train$sale_price - cv_pred(f5, train)
r6 <- train$sale_price - cv_pred(f6, train)
r7 <- train$sale_price - cv_pred(f7, train)

mi1 <- moran.mc(r1, lw, nsim = 999)
mi2 <- moran.mc(r2, lw, nsim = 999)
mi3 <- moran.mc(r3, lw, nsim = 999)
mi4 <- moran.mc(r4, lw, nsim = 999)
mi5 <- moran.mc(r5, lw, nsim = 999)
mi6 <- moran.mc(r6, lw, nsim = 999)
mi7 <- moran.mc(r7, lw, nsim = 999)

tibb <- tibble(
  model   = c("m1", "m2", "m3", "m4", "m5", "m6", "m7"),
  added   = c("Structure-only baseline",
              "+ bedrooms, fireplaces",
              "log1p(bedrooms)",
              "+ age squared",
              "+ distance to the Loop",
              "+ tract income, % poverty",
              "+ community area"),
  cv_rmse = c(rmse1, rmse2, rmse3, rmse4, rmse5, rmse6, rmse7),
  moran_i = c(mi1$statistic, mi2$statistic, mi3$statistic, mi4$statistic,
              mi5$statistic, mi6$statistic, mi7$statistic),
  notes   = c("Size, age and lot: features that needed little cleaning",
              "Details of the house beyond its size",
              "Each extra bedroom should add less than the one before",
              "Age plot in Part 1 curves: new and historic homes both sell higher",
              "Residual maps of m1-m4 were clustered: the model needed location",
              "Price map follows neighborhood income, not just distance downtown",
              "Fixed effect for each neighborhood's unmeasured amenities")
)
```

**Answer:** What helped most, and what disappointed you? Use your log.

*Your answer:*

Location helped most. The structure-only baseline (m1) had a CV RMSE of $301,503 and a Moran's I of 0.455. The house-feature steps (m2–m4: bedrooms, fireplaces, logged bedrooms, age squared) only brought CV RMSE down to $288,721, about $12,800 in total. The three location steps together cut it by almost $70,000. The community-area fixed effect (m7) was the biggest single step, cutting CV RMSE by about $36,700 and Moran's I from 0.422 to 0.263. Tract income and poverty (m6) came second, cutting CV RMSE by about $24,600; distance to the Loop (m5) added about $8,000. Our final model (m7) has a CV RMSE of $219,363 and a Moran's I of 0.263.

Three things disappointed us. Logging bedrooms, which we expected to help, changed CV RMSE by less than $600. Distance to the Loop lowered CV RMSE but slightly *raised* Moran's I (0.459 to 0.476), so on its own it did not fix the clustering. And even the final model leaves Moran's I well above zero, so nearby homes are still wrong in the same direction.

The residual maps show what changed. In the baseline map, a large red cluster runs along the North Side lakefront (Lincoln Park, Lake View, North Center): the model under-predicts the city's most expensive area because it does not know where homes are. In the final map, most of the city is close to zero and that north/south pattern is gone. The large errors that remain are still along the North Side lakefront, but now in both directions, with red and blue points next to each other. The model now knows the neighborhood, but not which homes within it are the top-end ones.

*Your answers:*

**4A.** The model fails worst along the North Side lakefront. Lincoln Park, Near North Side and Lake View have the largest average errors of any community area (about $622,000 per home in Lincoln Park, where the median sale is $1.6 million). Every community area's *average* residual is close to zero, because the community-area fixed effect absorbs it. The errors show up inside these neighborhoods, and they go in both directions:

- **Too low** in tracts where the most expensive homes sell, such as parts of Lake View, Lincoln Park and West Town (median sales around $1.7–3.3 million). In the worst tract, in Lincoln Park (median sale $3.3 million), homes sold for about $655,000 more than predicted on average.
- **Too high** in other tracts of the same neighborhoods, such as parts of Lincoln Park and the Near North Side, where homes are cheaper for the area (median around $0.8–1.3 million). In the worst tract, homes sold for about $605,000 less than predicted on average. The same thing happens far from the lakefront: in one Greater Grand Crossing tract, where the median sale is $70,000, homes sold for about $347,000 less than predicted.

We think this happens because the community-area fixed effect gives every home in a neighborhood the same location premium. In most of the city that works, because prices within a neighborhood are similar. On the North Side lakefront, prices range from under $1 million to over $4 million, and nothing in our model tells a $3 million home from a $900,000 one on the next block except its size, age and lot. So the model pushes both toward the neighborhood average: the top-end homes are under-valued and the more modest ones are over-valued.

**4B.** Only slightly, and not in the direction we expected. In the final model, the median ratio is 0.93 for homes in the lowest-income fifth of tracts and 1.03 in the highest, rising fairly steadily in between. If anything, homes in richer tracts are slightly over-valued. At the tract level, the poverty coefficient is −0.0040 (p < 0.001): each one-point rise in a tract's poverty rate *lowers* its median ratio by about 0.4%. Poverty explains under 3% of the variation in tract ratios (R² = 0.027). In our first draft, which had no location features, the same regression gave a coefficient of +0.026, with ratios rising about 2.6% per point of poverty. Adding tract income and poverty to the model removed that neighborhood-level bias, because the model now knows which neighborhoods are poorer.

The pattern by sale price is a different story. The cheapest tenth of homes have a median ratio of 1.88, while the most expensive tenth have 0.92. This is the same pattern "The Tax Divide" found in Cook County: lower-value homes are assessed at a higher share of their worth. Our location features fixed the bias *between* neighborhoods, but not the bias between cheap and expensive homes *within* them.

Our cleaning rules connect to this in both directions. At the top, our first draft dropped every sale over $1 million, which hid the expensive end of the market; keeping those sales gave the model a more honest view of it. At the bottom, we kept every sale, including about 170 sales under $30,000. Some of these may be foreclosures or other distressed sales rather than true market sales, and they push the ratio for the cheapest decile up sharply. We had no rule that could tell them apart from real low-priced sales, so we left them in. An Assessor faces the same choice. If this model were used for assessments, owners of the cheapest homes would be over-assessed the most, and they would pay a larger share of the tax bill.

## Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)

1. **Read one coefficient twice:** once as β̂, once for what it does to ŷ.
2. **Would you hand this model to the Assessor?** What would you warn them about?

*Your answer:*

Our final model enters bedrooms as log1p(num_bedrooms). As β̂, the coefficient is −$43,883: the change in predicted price for a one-unit increase in log(1 + bedrooms), holding living area, age, lot size, fireplaces and location fixed. On its own that is hard to use, since nobody adds "one log unit" of bedrooms to a house.

For ŷ, going from 2 to 3 bedrooms raises log1p by log(4/3) ≈ 0.29, which lowers the prediction by about $12,600. Going from 4 to 5 bedrooms raises it by only log(6/5) ≈ 0.18, which lowers the prediction by about $8,000. Each extra bedroom matters less than the one before. Because living area is held fixed, the negative sign means that splitting the same space into more, smaller rooms lowers the predicted price.

We would not hand this model to the Assessor yet. Adding location cut CV RMSE from $301,503 to $219,363, but three problems remain. First, Moran's I is still 0.263, so errors are still clustered: on the North Side lakefront, whole blocks of top-end homes are under-valued while their cheaper neighbors are over-valued. Second, the model is regressive. The cheapest tenth of homes are predicted at 1.88 times their sale price and the most expensive tenth at 0.92, which is the "Tax Divide" pattern. Adding location removed the bias by neighborhood poverty, but not this one: owners of cheaper homes, in every part of the city, would get relatively higher tax bills. Third, a linear model in dollars can predict prices that make no sense: 110 test homes were predicted below $10,000 (some below zero) and had to be set to a floor.

Before using it, we would add features that capture variation inside neighborhoods (transit access, crime, distance to the lake) and test the ratio by price and income again after every change.
